title: Part Two, Chapter 2: The Journey to the Underworld and the Death of the Two Brothers

verses.t: And then came the messengers of Hun-came and Vucub-came. "Go," they said to them, "you chief lords; go and call Hun-hun-ahpu and Vucub-hun-ahpu, and tell them to come here to us. Tell them that the lords say they are to come and play here, to come and entertain us, because truly their doings amaze us. So let them come, for the lords say so, and let them bring all the gear of their game: the bat and the ring; and let them also bring the rubber ball. Tell them that the lords say so." So it was said to the messengers. And the messengers were owls: an arrow owl, a one-legged owl, a macaw owl and a head owl; these were the names of the messengers of the underworld. The one called arrow owl was like an arrow, and alert; the one called one-legged had only one leg, and had wings; the one called macaw owl had a red back, and had wings; the one called owl's head had nothing but a head; it had no feet, only wings. These four messengers were chief lords. Then they came from the underworld with the message, and in an instant they arrived straight at the court where Hun-hun-ahpu and Vucub-hun-ahpu were playing ball; and the court was called Nim-xob-carchan. And the four owls who had been sent gave their message and embassy from Hun-came and Vucub-came, from Ahalpuh, Ahalcana, Chamiabac and Chamia-holom, Xiquiripat, Cuchumaquic, Ahalmez, Ahaltocob, Xic and Patán; these were their names. And when the message had been given, the brothers said, "Is it really so? Do the lord Came and Vucub-came say this?" "It is true," said the messengers. "And are we to go with you?" "Bring all the gear, for so the lords say." "Very well," they said, "wait for us while we go and tell our mother." And then they went to their house and said to their mother, for their father was already dead, "Mother, we are going, but our going will be in vain. The messenger of the lords has come for us; the lords say that we are to go." They went and hung the rubber ball up in the loft of the house, and as they came back they said, "We shall play again." And they said to their sons Hun-batz and Hun-choven, "You, by yourselves, pass the time playing the flute, singing, painting and carving. Stay here; keep our house warm, and keep your grandmother's heart warm." And when they said this, the heart of their mother Xmucane was very tender, and she wept. "Come, do not cry, do not grieve," they said to her. "We are going; we shall not die." And then Hun-hun-ahpu and Vucub-hun-ahpu went away. And as soon as Hun-hun-ahpu and Vucub-hun-ahpu had gone, the messengers took the lead, and then they went down by the road to the underworld, whose steps were very steep. And they went down, and when they came out they reached the rushing water, a very narrow ravine called the strong ravine; and passing on from there to the water that changes, they passed where everything was sharp stakes, and they were not wounded. On the bank of a river that was of blood they did not drink from the river, nor could they be defeated; they crossed over and came to a road that divided into four roads, and there at the crossroads they were defeated. One road was red, another black, another white and another yellow. And as they stood perplexed, the black road spoke: "You must take me, for I am the road of the lords." And there they were beaten; and following this road they came to the thrones of the lords of the underworld, and there they were beaten. The first one seated was a man carved and dressed up by those of the underworld, and he was the first they greeted, saying, "Good day, lord Hun-came; are you well, lord Vucub-came?" But he did not answer them. And then the lords of the underworld began to make a great noise, laughing; and again all the lords made noise, laughing, because the brothers had been beaten, and in their hearts they had already defeated Hun-hun-ahpu and Vucub-hun-ahpu; and they laughed. And then Hun-came and Vucub-came said to them, "Very well; you have come. Tomorrow prepare the ring, the bat and the rest. Now come and sit on our bench." And the bench was of burning stone, and as they sat down they were burned on the seat; and they turned about, but they did not get up; they squirmed, and their buttocks were burned. And then those of the underworld laughed again; they were dying of laughter, their insides ached with laughing, they were about to burst with blood, and the bones of all the lords of the underworld were coming out of them with laughter.

"Come, go to that house," they said to them, "and there your torch of pine will be brought to you." And then they went to the house of darkness, where there was only darkness in that house. And then the lords of the underworld considered what they should do, and what they decided was to cut them to pieces soon, the next day: "They will die soon, through that fire of theirs and through their ball." This they discussed among themselves. And their torch was made of a kind of stone from which knives are made, which is called saquitoc ("sharp piercer"), and the torch was pointed and sharp.

And the pine torch of those of the underworld was very hard. And Hun-hun-ahpu and Vucub-hun-ahpu went into that dark house, and then they went to give them their torch; only one lighted torch was what Hun-came and Vucub-came sent them, and along with it two rolls of tobacco or cigars were what the lords sent and gave to Hun-hun-ahpu and Vucub-hun-ahpu. And when those who carried the torch arrived, the brothers were crouched and huddled in the darkness, and the torch came in shining. "Light the cigar," say the lords; "tomorrow you must return them, with the torch, without their being used up. This is what the lords say." And there they were beaten, because they used up the torch and the tobacco that had been given them. Many were the punishments that those of the underworld had, and many kinds of punishments. The first was that dark house, where there was only darkness; the second was called the house where they shivered, where there was only great cold, a cold most intolerable and unbearable; the third was the house of jaguars, where there were only jaguars, where they could hardly stir, and there they jostled and bit each other; the fourth was the house of bats, where there were only bats, shrieking and flying about shut in, unable to get out; the fifth was the house of obsidian knives, where there were only these knives with very sharp edges, which kept clashing and grinding against one another. Many were the punishments of the underworld, but Hun-hun-ahpu and Vucub-hun-ahpu did not enter them; these punishments will be told of later. And when Hun-hun-ahpu and Vucub-hun-ahpu came before Hun-came and Vucub-came, these said to them, "Where are the tobacco and the torch that were given you last night?" They answered, "Lord, we used them up." "Very well," said Hun-came and Vucub-came. "Your days are finished now; you shall die, and you shall be destroyed; here you shall be broken, and your faces shall stay hidden here." And then they were cut to pieces and buried where the ashes were thrown; and the head of Hun-hun-ahpu was cut off, and only his body was buried with his brother. And then Hun-came and Vucub-came ordered it to be placed in the fork of a tree by the road, and then they placed the head in a fork; and then that tree bore fruit, which had had no fruit before the head of Hun-hun-ahpu was placed in the fork. And what it bore is what we now call calabashes (Crescentia): the head of Hun-hun-ahpu. And seeing this, Hun-came and Vucub-came marvelled at the fruit of the tree, which was covered all over with that round fruit; and then it could no longer be told where the head of Hun-hun-ahpu was, for it had become all one with the calabashes; so it seemed to the eyes of all those of the underworld when they went to amuse themselves. They held that tree in great esteem, because it had been made in an instant, when they placed the head of Hun-hun-ahpu in the fork. And they said to one another, "Let no one pick this fruit or stand beneath the tree." So all those of the underworld ordered and decreed, and no one could see where the head of Hun-hun-ahpu was, because it had become all one with the calabashes. And a maiden heard of this wonder; now we shall tell how she went there.
